title: Cranberry Sauce

drivers.name: Price increase (2.7%)
drivers.evidence: Price rose from $2.78 to $2.85. Past promotions show lift only when discounting; no prior data on price increase impact, but post-promo weeks show x0.68 (noise-adjusted x1.0), implying demand is sensitive to price. Use moderate downward adjustment.

adjustment.analysis: Baseline median is 8.6. No events in target week. Price increased to $2.85 (+2.7% vs $2.78). Past promotions show average lift of x1.53, but noise-adjusted estimate is x1.0. The most recent promotion (30% off, 2026-02-23) lifted sales to x1.48, but this was a deep discount not repeated. The price increase is a demand suppressor. The week after promotions typically sees x0.68 sales (noise-adjusted x1.0), suggesting no lasting pull-forward. Mother's Day (week before) had mixed results (x0.26, x1.9), noise-adjusted x1.0. No evidence of sustained demand shift. Adjust for price increase: expect mild downward pressure. Confidence is medium due to limited past price effect data.

PRODUCT: Cranberry Sauce | category Grocery | Store #12 (Austin, TX)
TARGET WEEK: 2026-04-27 to 2026-05-03 (next week)

KNOWN PLAN FOR THE TARGET WEEK:
  events: none
  shelf price: 2.85 (+2.7% vs regular price 2.78)

STATISTICAL BASELINE (exponential smoothing of recent sales; it ignores events, promotions and prices):
  median 8.6 | 5%-95%: 0.0 - 18.7 | 10%-90%: 1.1 - 17.2

In the evidence below, 'vs baseline' = actual units / what this same baseline predicted for that week.
It is the multiplier that would have been right, so it maps directly onto median_multiplier.
This product's ordinary weeks already swing about +/-74% around the baseline, so a past effect smaller than that, seen only a few times, is mostly noise. The
'noise-adjusted estimate' is the effect shrunk toward x1.0 for that noise and the number of sightings.
